sections.title: Twelve sailors and two oranges
sections.intro_md:
On 20 May 1747, in the Bay of Biscay, a 31-year-old naval surgeon named **James Lind** picked twelve men with the same disease, gave them the same breakfast, the same dinner and the same hammock deck, and then changed exactly one thing for each pair. Six remedies, two men each, fourteen days.

The pair who got two oranges and a lemon a day were back on their feet within a week. Nobody else recovered much. It looks obvious now. It was not obvious then, and here is the strange part: Lind himself did not fully believe his own result, and the Royal Navy took **48 more years** to give its sailors lemon juice as routine. Scurvy killed more British sailors in the 18th century than enemy action did.

This day is about the idea Lind stumbled toward: that you cannot tell whether a treatment works by trusting the doctor, the patient or the story. You have to build a **fair test**. It took medicine about two centuries to learn how, and the lessons were paid for in blood, sometimes literally.

spotlights.name: James Lind
spotlights.spot_it: Scottish naval surgeon in an 18th-century wig, later chief physician of Haslar naval hospital near Portsmouth.
spotlights.story_md: Lind joined the navy as a surgeon's mate at 23 and saw scurvy up close: bleeding gums, old wounds reopening, men too weak to climb rigging. After his 1747 test he went home to Edinburgh, took a medical degree and in 1753 published **A Treatise of the Scurvy**, 456 pages long. The famous experiment takes up barely a page. Most of the book reviews every earlier theory, and Lind still thought scurvy came from damp air and blocked perspiration. He even boiled lemon juice down into a concentrate called a 'rob', which destroyed most of its vitamin C. He ran Haslar, then the largest hospital in Britain, until 1783.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He ran the first well-recorded controlled comparison of treatments, even if he misread what it meant.
spotlights.memory_hook: The man who proved oranges worked, then boiled the cure out of them.

spotlights.name: The HMS Salisbury scurvy test
spotlights.spot_it: Six pairs of sick sailors, six remedies, one shared diet: the pattern every comparative trial still follows.
spotlights.story_md: Lind's six treatments were a quart of cider a day, 25 drops of 'elixir of vitriol' (dilute sulphuric acid), six spoonfuls of vinegar, half a pint of seawater, two oranges and a lemon, and a spicy paste of garlic, mustard and horseradish with barley water. Everything else was held the same, which is the clever bit. The citrus pair improved fastest: one was fit for duty after six days, when the fruit ran out, and was put to nursing the others. The cider pair improved a little. Lind did not randomise, did not blind and had only two men per group, so by modern standards it is an anecdote with a control. But it was a deliberate, prospective comparison, written down.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows the core logic of a trial: hold everything equal, change one thing, compare.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six pairs, one variable, and the lemons won.

spotlights.name: Scurvy
spotlights.spot_it: Swollen, purple, bleeding gums, loose teeth and bruises that appear without injury.
spotlights.story_md: Scurvy is vitamin C deficiency. Without vitamin C the body cannot make proper collagen, the protein that holds skin, gums and blood vessels together, so tissues literally come apart. On Vasco da Gama's 1497 voyage to India, many of his crew died of it. On George Anson's voyage round the world from 1740, about 1,400 of roughly 1,900 men died, most from disease and scurvy chief among them. The cure was found and lost repeatedly because nobody knew why it worked. Vitamin C itself was isolated by **Albert Szent-Györgyi** in Hungary in 1932, and he won the Nobel Prize in 1937.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the disease that made the first famous controlled test necessary.
spotlights.memory_hook: Collagen is the glue; without vitamin C, the body comes unglued.

spotlights.name: The Navy finally issues lemon juice
spotlights.spot_it: Royal Navy sailors queuing for a daily ration of lemon juice mixed into their grog.
spotlights.story_md: In 1794, at the insistence of Rear Admiral Alan Gardner, the ship HMS Suffolk carried lemon juice on a 23-week voyage to India. Not one man got serious scurvy. In 1795 the Admiralty adopted the Sick and Hurt Board's advice and issued lemon juice across the fleet. Physicians **Gilbert Blane** and Thomas Trotter had pushed for it. Later the Navy switched to cheaper West Indian limes, which have far less vitamin C, and scurvy crept back into polar expeditions in the 1870s. The nickname 'limey' for British sailors survives from that switch.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that evidence alone does not change practice; institutions have to act on it.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty-eight years from proof to policy, then a cheaper fruit undid it.

sections.title: What a fair test actually is
sections.intro_md:
A **clinical trial** is an experiment on people that compares one way of treating them with another. The modern gold standard is the **randomised controlled trial (RCT)**, and its parts are easy to name.

**A control group** gets the old treatment, a dummy treatment (a **placebo**) or nothing, so you can see what would have happened anyway. Many illnesses get better on their own, and many patients feel better just from being cared for.

**Randomisation** decides by chance who gets what, so that the doctor's hopes cannot steer the healthier patients into the new treatment.

**Blinding** hides who got what, from the patient (single blind) and also from the doctors judging the results (double blind).

**Enough people**, counted in advance, so that a real effect stands out from luck.

Each of these parts was invented separately, usually after someone was fooled by its absence. Put together, they let a test answer one question honestly: did this treatment cause that outcome?

spotlights.name: The randomised controlled trial
spotlights.spot_it: Two or more groups formed by chance, treated differently, measured the same way, with the outcome judged by someone who does not know which group is which.
spotlights.story_md: The trick of randomisation is that it balances what you cannot see. A doctor can match groups by age and sex, but not by genes, grit, diet or luck. Toss a coin for each patient and, with enough patients, all those hidden factors spread evenly across groups. Any difference left at the end is then very likely due to the treatment. RCTs have since escaped medicine: economists use them to test school programmes, cash transfers and microfinance, and the 2019 economics Nobel went to Abhijit Banerjee, Esther Duflo and Michael Kremer for doing exactly that, often in India.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the one design that handles the confounders nobody thought to measure.
spotlights.memory_hook: Chance is the only referee that cannot be bribed.

spotlights.name: The placebo
spotlights.when: Word in medical use from the 1780s
spotlights.spot_it: A sugar pill, saline injection or sham procedure made to look exactly like the real treatment.
spotlights.story_md: Placebo is Latin for 'I shall please'. In medieval church usage it named the vespers for the dead, sung by hired mourners, and by the 18th century doctors used it for any medicine given more to please than to cure. In a trial the placebo has a very specific job: it makes the comparison group live through the same ritual, the pill, the injection, the attention, so that the only difference left is the active ingredient. Without it, a drug gets credit for the comfort of being treated. Surgeons have even used **sham operations**, small incisions with nothing done inside, to test whether the real surgery adds anything.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Without a believable dummy, hope and attention get counted as cure.
spotlights.memory_hook: Placebo means 'I shall please', and pleasing is exactly what it must not get credit for.

sections.title: Two thousand years of trusting the doctor
sections.intro_md:
For most of history, medicine ran on **authority**: what Hippocrates, Galen or your teacher said, plus what you had seen work. That sounds reasonable until you see what it produced. Bloodletting, purging and blistering were standard care for over 2,000 years, mostly because patients who survived them were remembered and patients who died were blamed on the disease.

Yet sparks of the fair-test idea appear early. A Biblical story compares two diets. A Persian physician wrote rules for testing drugs a thousand years ago. A French army surgeon ran out of boiling oil and noticed something. None of these became a method. They show that the idea is old and simple, and that the hard part was getting anyone to act on it.

spotlights.name: Daniel's ten-day diet test
spotlights.when: Book of Daniel, written about the 2nd century BCE
spotlights.spot_it: A captive youth in Babylon asks a royal steward for a ten-day comparison: vegetables and water against the king's rich food.
spotlights.story_md: In chapter 1 of the Book of Daniel, Daniel and three companions refuse the meat and wine from Nebuchadnezzar's table. The steward fears they will look weaker than the other young men. Daniel proposes a test: 'Prove thy servants, I beseech thee, ten days', give us pulses and water, then compare our faces with those who eat the king's food. After ten days they look healthier, and the steward switches everyone. It has a comparison group, a fixed time and an outcome checked by a sceptic. The James Lind Library, the main archive of fair-test history, opens its collection with it.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the oldest well-known written description of a planned comparison.
spotlights.memory_hook: Ten days, two diets, one sceptical steward.

spotlights.name: Avicenna's rules for testing drugs
spotlights.spot_it: A thick Arabic medical encyclopaedia, copied and printed across Europe and Asia for 600 years.
spotlights.story_md: Ibn Sina, known in Europe as Avicenna, was a Persian physician and philosopher. In Book 2 of his **Canon of Medicine** he set out seven rules for judging a drug. Test it on a simple, uncomplicated disease, not a mixture. Test it on two opposite types of illness. Check that the effect is the same each time. Make sure the timing fits, so the cure did not just coincide with the illness ending. And test it on humans, because a drug that works on a lion or a horse may not work on a man. The Canon remained a standard text in European universities until about the 17th century.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He wrote down the logic of controlled testing nearly 750 years before Lind.
spotlights.memory_hook: Seven rules, a lion and a horse, a thousand years ago.

spotlights.name: Ambroise Paré and the boiling oil
spotlights.spot_it: A French barber-surgeon who became royal surgeon to four kings of France.
spotlights.story_md: Surgeons of Paré's time believed gunshot wounds were poisoned by gunpowder, so they poured boiling elder oil into them. At the siege of Turin in 1537, the young Paré ran out of oil. He improvised a dressing of egg yolk, oil of roses and turpentine and expected those soldiers to die. He slept badly and rose early to check. The men given his dressing had little pain and no swelling. The ones scalded with oil were feverish and in agony. He never used boiling oil again. It was an accidental comparison, but he noticed it and wrote it down.
spotlights.why_it_matters: An unplanned control group overturned a cruel standard treatment.
spotlights.memory_hook: He ran out of boiling oil and found mercy worked better.

spotlights.name: George Washington is bled to death
spotlights.spot_it: The first US President on his deathbed, surrounded by doctors.
spotlights.story_md: Washington woke with a severe sore throat after riding in sleet. Over about 12 hours his doctors bled him four times, taking an estimated 2.4 litres, roughly 40% of his blood, plus blistering and purges. He died that night aged 67. Most historians now think he had acute epiglottitis, a swelling that blocks the airway, and the bleeding probably hastened his death. Nobody at the time could prove that, because no one had ever tested bloodletting fairly. That test came 36 years later in Paris.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how a treatment with no evidence could still be given to the most powerful man in a country.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four bleedings in a day for a sore throat: standard care in 1799.

sections.title: Doctors who started counting
sections.intro_md:
The 19th century gave medicine a new habit: **counting**. Instead of remembering striking cases, a few doctors began to tally outcomes in groups and compare rates. This is the 'numerical method', and it was deeply unpopular. Many physicians said each patient was unique and that statistics insulted the art of medicine.

The numbers won anyway, slowly. A Paris doctor counted bloodletting deaths. A Hungarian obstetrician counted deaths on two maternity wards. A London anaesthetist counted cholera deaths by water company. A nurse drew a chart that changed how armies ran hospitals. None of these were randomised trials. Some were natural experiments, where chance or history had already made two comparable groups. All of them showed that a count can see what a clinician's memory cannot.

visual.title: Semmelweis's two wards: mothers dying after childbirth (%)

spotlights.name: Pierre Louis counts the bled
spotlights.spot_it: A Paris hospital physician with ledgers of patient outcomes, scorned by colleagues as a mere counter.
spotlights.story_md: Pierre-Charles-Alexandre Louis studied 77 pneumonia patients at La Charité hospital and compared those bled early in the illness with those bled later. Of 41 bled in the first four days, 18 died, about 44%. Of 36 bled later, 9 died, 25%. His 1835 book on bloodletting argued it did far less good than believed. His method spread more than his conclusion: American students who trained with him in Paris carried the 'numerical method' home, and bloodletting slowly declined over the following decades.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that a common treatment had to answer to numbers, not reputation.
spotlights.memory_hook: Louis put bloodletting in a ledger, and the ledger said no.

spotlights.name: Ignaz Semmelweis and the two wards
spotlights.spot_it: A Hungarian doctor who ordered staff to wash their hands in chlorinated lime before examining mothers.
spotlights.story_md: Vienna General Hospital had two maternity clinics, and women were admitted to them on alternate days, an accidental fair split. The ward run by doctors and medical students killed about five times as many mothers from childbed fever as the ward run by midwives. Women begged to give birth in the street rather than be admitted to it. In 1847 Semmelweis guessed that students carried 'cadaverous particles' from the autopsy room. He brought in chlorine handwashing and deaths on the doctors' ward fell to the midwives' level. Colleagues rejected him. He died in an asylum in 1865, aged 47.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a natural experiment that revealed doctors were spreading the disease they treated.
spotlights.memory_hook: Same city, same hospital, alternate days: the doctors' ward was the dangerous one.

spotlights.name: John Snow's 'grand experiment'
spotlights.spot_it: A map of Soho with black bars stacked at each house where someone died of cholera, clustered round one water pump.
spotlights.story_md: Snow is famous for the Broad Street pump, whose handle was removed on 8 September 1854. His stronger evidence came from water companies. In south London two companies piped water to the same streets, often to neighbouring houses. Southwark and Vauxhall drew water from the Thames downstream of the city's sewage; Lambeth had moved its intake upstream in 1852. Households could not choose and did not know. Snow found cholera deaths were about 315 per 10,000 houses for Southwark and Vauxhall customers against 37 for Lambeth. It was a randomised experiment that history ran for him.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A natural experiment proved cholera spread through water decades before the germ was seen.
spotlights.memory_hook: Two pipes, one street, eight times the deaths.

spotlights.name: Florence Nightingale's rose diagram
spotlights.spot_it: A circular chart of wedges, blue for deaths from preventable disease, dwarfing the red wedges for wounds.
spotlights.story_md: In the Crimean War hospital at Scutari, Nightingale found soldiers were far more likely to die of infection, cholera and dysentery than of battle wounds. Back in Britain she worked with the statistician William Farr and in 1858 published her 'Diagram of the Causes of Mortality in the Army in the East'. Each wedge is a month; its area shows deaths. The huge blue wedges made the point that numbers in a table could not: sanitation was killing more men than Russian guns. She became the first woman elected to the Royal Statistical Society, in 1858.
spotlights.why_it_matters: She showed that data presented clearly can force institutions to change.
spotlights.memory_hook: Blue wedges for dirt, red wedges for bullets, and blue won the war.

sections.title: How a fake cure invented the blind test
sections.intro_md:
**Blinding** was not invented to test a medicine. It was invented to expose a fraud. In 1780s Paris, the fashionable cure was 'animal magnetism', and the King of France wanted to know whether it was real. The commission he appointed, with Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier among its members, did something new: it tested patients who did not know whether they were being treated.

Fifteen years later, an English doctor did the same to a patented American cure, using fakes made of wood. Both tests reached the same conclusion: the effect was in the patient's expectation, not in the device. That insight is the reason modern trials hide who gets the real drug.

spotlights.name: Franz Anton Mesmer and the baquet
spotlights.spot_it: A wooden tub with iron rods sticking out, patients holding the rods and roped together in a circle.
spotlights.story_md: Mesmer, a Viennese physician, claimed that an invisible fluid flowed through all living things and that illness came from blockages. In Paris he treated wealthy patients around the **baquet**, a covered tub filled with water and iron filings, while soft music played and Mesmer, in a lilac silk coat, pointed an iron wand. Patients often had 'crises', fits of shaking and crying, and then reported relief. He charged high fees and drew huge crowds. One of the few surviving original baquets is in Lyon's municipal library collection.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Mesmerism's real effects were so convincing that only a blind test could separate belief from mechanism.
spotlights.memory_hook: A tub of iron filings, a lilac coat and a whole city in a trance.

spotlights.name: The Franklin commission's blindfold tests
spotlights.spot_it: Elderly American ambassador Benjamin Franklin, then living in Passy near Paris, chairing royal scientists.
spotlights.story_md: Louis XVI set up two commissions in 1784. One included **Benjamin Franklin**, chemist **Antoine Lavoisier** and Dr Joseph-Ignace Guillotin. They blindfolded subjects and told them they were being magnetised when they were not, and the reverse. Effects followed belief, not treatment. In Franklin's garden at Passy, a boy was told one apricot tree had been magnetised. He walked from tree to tree and fainted at the fourth, which had not been touched. The commission concluded the effects came from 'imagination'. It is widely counted as the first blind, sham-controlled test.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It created the blind test and showed that expectation alone can produce dramatic physical effects.
spotlights.memory_hook: The boy fainted under the wrong apricot tree.

spotlights.name: Perkins's tractors and Haygarth's wooden fakes
spotlights.spot_it: A pair of three-inch metal rods, one brass-coloured and one iron-coloured, stroked over the painful part.
spotlights.story_md: Elisha Perkins, a Connecticut doctor, patented his 'metallic tractors' in 1796 and sold them for five guineas a pair, claiming they drew disease out through electrical fluid. George Washington is said to have bought a set. In 1799 Dr **John Haygarth** of Bath made fake tractors out of wood, painted to look like metal. He used them on five patients with rheumatism; four reported relief, just as with the real ones. In 1800 he published 'Of the Imagination, as a Cause and as a Cure of Disorders of the Body'. It is often described as the first placebo-controlled test.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that the ritual of a treatment can relieve symptoms on its own.
spotlights.memory_hook: Painted wood cured as well as patented metal.

compare.difference: Both were tested blind or with fakes; both effects turned out to live in the patient's expectation.

sections.title: Letting chance decide
sections.intro_md:
Controls and blinding were not enough. If a doctor chooses who gets the new treatment, he will tend, often without knowing it, to give it to patients he thinks will do well. The fix is to take the choice away from people and give it to **chance**.

The idea came from several places at once. A Danish doctor alternated a new serum by day of admission. Two American philosophers used a shuffled deck of cards to test human perception. A British statistician working on wheat fields made randomisation the foundation of experimental design. By the 1930s the mathematics existed. Medicine only needed someone willing to apply it to sick people.

spotlights.name: Johannes Fibiger's diphtheria serum test
spotlights.spot_it: A Danish doctor who gave antitoxin serum to patients admitted on one day and withheld it on the next.
spotlights.story_md: Diphtheria antitoxin had just arrived, and doctors disagreed fiercely about it. At Copenhagen's Blegdam hospital, **Johannes Fibiger** gave serum to patients admitted on alternate days and treated the others normally, about 484 patients in all. Eight serum patients died against 30 in the comparison group. Alternation is not true randomisation, because staff can know the schedule, but it removed most of the doctor's choice. Fibiger later won the 1926 Nobel Prize for a cancer discovery that turned out to be wrong, while his trial, which is right, is the work historians now praise.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It was one of the first trials to take allocation out of the doctor's hands.
spotlights.memory_hook: His Nobel was a mistake; his trial was a masterpiece.

spotlights.name: Ronald Fisher
spotlights.spot_it: A short-sighted English statistician and geneticist with round glasses and a pipe, who worked out experiments on wheat plots.
spotlights.story_md: At Rothamsted from 1919, Fisher was handed decades of crop data that could not answer basic questions, because the plots had not been laid out by chance. He argued that randomising which plot gets which fertiliser is the only way to make the error estimate valid. His 1935 book **The Design of Experiments** opens with a lady who claims she can tell whether milk or tea was poured first. Fisher designs the test: eight cups, four of each, served in random order. Its logic, the null hypothesis and the p-value, still runs nearly every trial. Fisher also defended tobacco and argued against the smoking-cancer link, while consulting for the industry.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He supplied the mathematics that makes randomised experiments trustworthy.
spotlights.memory_hook: Eight cups of tea built the modern experiment.

spotlights.name: Broadbalk field, Rothamsted
spotlights.spot_it: A long English wheat field striped into strips that each get a different fertiliser, every year since 1843.
spotlights.story_md: The **Broadbalk** experiment at Rothamsted in Harpenden, north of London, is one of the oldest continuous field experiments in the world. John Lawes and Henry Gilbert started it to test manures and fertilisers on winter wheat. Its strips were laid out systematically, not by chance, which is part of what frustrated Fisher when he arrived. The field taught him why experiments need randomisation and replication, lessons that crossed from agriculture to medicine. It is still sown and harvested, more than 180 years on.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The design of modern medical trials began in a wheat field.
spotlights.memory_hook: Medicine's best method grew out of English wheat.

sections.title: 1948: the trial that started it all
sections.intro_md:
On 30 October 1948 the British Medical Journal published a paper usually counted as the first properly randomised controlled trial in medicine: **streptomycin in pulmonary tuberculosis**, run by Britain's Medical Research Council.

It happened because of a shortage. The US had discovered streptomycin, a new antibiotic, and Britain could afford only a tiny amount after the war. Some patients would get the drug and some would not, whatever anyone decided. The statistician **Austin Bradford Hill** argued that the fairest way to choose was by chance, and that the result would answer the question properly. Rationing made the control group ethical.

The same team then turned the method on a new problem. Using careful comparison of groups, though not randomisation, Hill and a young doctor named Richard Doll showed that smoking causes lung cancer.

visual.title: MRC streptomycin trial, 1948: died within six months (%)

spotlights.name: The MRC streptomycin trial
spotlights.spot_it: 107 young adults with severe TB of both lungs, allocated by numbers sealed in opaque envelopes.
spotlights.story_md: Patients aged 15 to 30 with acute bilateral tuberculosis were assigned by a list of random numbers that Hill drew up and that clinicians never saw; each allocation sat in a sealed envelope opened only after a patient was enrolled. 55 got streptomycin and bed rest, 52 got bed rest alone. The chest X-rays were read by radiologists who did not know the allocation. After six months, 4 of the streptomycin group had died against 14 of the controls. The trial also revealed a problem: TB bacteria quickly became resistant to streptomycin used alone, which led to combination therapy.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It set the template: concealed random allocation, blinded assessment, pre-set outcomes.
spotlights.memory_hook: Sealed envelopes, opaque to everyone, including the doctors.

spotlights.name: Austin Bradford Hill
spotlights.spot_it: A London statistician with no medical degree who taught doctors how to think about evidence.
spotlights.story_md: Hill wanted to be a doctor, but tuberculosis, caught while serving as a pilot in the First World War, ended that plan. He took an economics degree by correspondence and turned to medical statistics. In 1937 he published a series of articles in The Lancet, 'Principles of Medical Statistics', that made the subject readable for clinicians. He chose to call his method 'random allocation' and avoided the word randomisation, fearing doctors would be put off by mathematics. In 1965 he set out nine viewpoints, now called the **Bradford Hill criteria**, for judging whether an association is causal.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned randomisation from statistical theory into a clinical routine.
spotlights.memory_hook: A failed medical student who taught medicine how to know.

spotlights.name: Selman Waksman and Albert Schatz
spotlights.spot_it: A soil microbiologist at Rutgers in New Jersey, pictured at the laboratory bench.
spotlights.story_md: Streptomycin came from a soil bacterium, Streptomyces griseus. It was isolated in 1943 in Waksman's lab by his graduate student **Albert Schatz**, who worked in a basement lab partly to keep the deadly TB germ away from others. Waksman alone received the 1952 Nobel Prize. Schatz sued in 1950 and won a settlement and recognition as co-discoverer, but was largely shut out of the field afterwards. The drug that launched the RCT was itself the subject of one of science's best-known credit disputes.
spotlights.why_it_matters: The drug at the centre of the first modern RCT is also a case study in who gets credit.
spotlights.memory_hook: A student found it in the soil; his professor got the Nobel.

spotlights.name: Richard Doll and the British Doctors Study
spotlights.spot_it: A London doctor who gave up smoking halfway through his own research.
spotlights.story_md: In 1950 Doll and Hill compared lung cancer patients with other patients in London hospitals and found the cancer patients were far more likely to be heavy smokers. Doll stopped smoking. To strengthen the case they wrote in 1951 to all British doctors, and about 40,000 replied with their smoking habits; the team then followed them for 50 years. Smokers died on average about ten years earlier than non-smokers. You cannot randomise people to smoke, so this was an observational cohort, yet it changed policy worldwide. It also showed the limits of trials: some questions need other kinds of evidence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved smoking kills and showed how to reason about causes when a trial is impossible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty thousand doctors and fifty years: smokers lost a decade.

sections.title: The biggest experiment ever: polio, 1954
sections.intro_md:
In the early 1950s polio terrified American parents. Swimming pools closed in summer. In 1952 the US recorded about 58,000 cases, and thousands of children were left paralysed or breathing through iron lungs. When **Jonas Salk** produced a killed-virus vaccine, the pressure to simply give it to everyone was enormous.

Instead, in 1954, the National Foundation for Infantile Paralysis, a charity funded by the March of Dimes, ran the **Francis Field Trial**: about 1.8 million children, of whom roughly 650,000 got injections, real or dummy, and about 1.2 million were observed. It was led by Salk's former teacher **Thomas Francis Jr.** at the University of Michigan. The announcement on 12 April 1955 was one of the great public events of the century. Then, within weeks, a manufacturing failure showed why safety testing never stops.

visual.title: Who was in the 1954 polio trial (share of about 1.8 million children)

spotlights.name: Jonas Salk
spotlights.spot_it: A New York-born virologist in a white coat, who became the most famous scientist in America overnight.
spotlights.story_md: Salk grew poliovirus in monkey kidney cells and killed it with formaldehyde, so it could train the immune system without causing disease. He tested it on himself, his wife and their three sons in 1953. Older virologists, notably Albert Sabin, thought a killed vaccine would be weak and preferred a live one. When asked on television in 1955 who owned the patent, Salk answered: 'Well, the people, I would say. There is no patent. Could you patent the sun?' Lawyers had in fact concluded it probably could not have been patented anyway.
spotlights.why_it_matters: His vaccine was the first to be proven in a giant controlled trial before mass use.
spotlights.memory_hook: Could you patent the sun?

spotlights.name: The Francis Field Trial

where.label: Rackham Auditorium, University of Michigan, Ann Arbor

spotlights.spot_it: Six-to-nine-year-olds in school lines receiving shots, each given a 'Polio Pioneer' certificate and pin.
spotlights.story_md: Thomas Francis insisted on a proper design. In 11 states, about 650,000 children were given either vaccine or a placebo of culture medium, with coded vials so nobody knew which, the gold-standard arm. In other areas, second-graders got vaccine and first and third graders were simply observed, a weaker design that politicians and parents preferred. Some 20,000 doctors and public health officers, 40,000 nurses and about 220,000 volunteers took part. The blinded arm showed the vaccine was about 80 to 90% effective against paralytic polio. Francis announced it at the University of Michigan on 12 April 1955, ten years to the day after President Roosevelt, polio's most famous patient, died.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved a vaccine in a huge blinded trial and set the standard for vaccine testing.
spotlights.memory_hook: Six hundred and fifty thousand coded vials, and nobody knew which was which.

spotlights.name: The iron lung
spotlights.spot_it: A metal cylinder the size of a car engine, with a child's head sticking out of one end.
spotlights.story_md: Polio can paralyse the muscles used for breathing. The **Drinker respirator**, built by Philip Drinker and Louis Agassiz Shaw at Harvard in 1928, changed the air pressure inside a sealed tank to pull air in and out of the patient's lungs. At the height of the epidemics, hospital wards held rows of them. Some patients spent decades inside; Paul Alexander of Texas, paralysed in 1952, lived in his until his death in 2024, and wrote a book with a pen held in his mouth. The iron lung is why the polio trial felt urgent to every parent.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the image of what the polio vaccine trial was racing to prevent.
spotlights.memory_hook: A metal lung, and a child's face in a mirror above it.

spotlights.name: The Cutter incident
spotlights.spot_it: Vaccine batches from one Californian laboratory that still contained live virus.
spotlights.story_md: Within two weeks of licensing, Cutter Laboratories of Berkeley shipped vaccine in which the virus had not been fully killed. About 120,000 doses contained live poliovirus. Some 40,000 children developed mild polio, 51 were permanently paralysed and 5 died. The virus then spread to families and neighbours, paralysing 113 more people and killing 5. The national programme was paused. The result was a new US federal system for checking vaccine batches. The lesson for trials is blunt: a product proven in a trial must still be made exactly as it was in the trial.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that safety does not end with a successful trial; manufacturing has to be tested too.
spotlights.memory_hook: A trial proves the recipe, not every batch.

sections.title: When the experiment was the crime
sections.intro_md:
The same decades that perfected the trial also produced its worst abuses. Fair tests need people, and for a long time the people chosen were those least able to say no: prisoners, the poor, soldiers, orphans, colonised and Black communities.

The rules we now take for granted were written in response to specific horrors. The **Nuremberg Code** of 1947 came out of the trial of Nazi doctors. The **Declaration of Helsinki**, first adopted by the World Medical Association in 1964 and revised most recently in October 2024, came from doctors wanting their own code. The US **Belmont Report** of 1979 came out of the Tuskegee scandal. The **1962 Kefauver-Harris law**, which first made drug companies prove that medicines work, passed because of thalidomide.

The common thread is **informed consent**: people must understand what is being done to them and be free to refuse. It sounds basic. It was not standard practice until well within living memory.

spotlights.name: The Doctors' Trial and the Nuremberg Code
spotlights.spot_it: Rows of defendants in headphones in a wood-panelled courtroom, many of them physicians in plain suits.
spotlights.story_md: Twenty-three defendants, twenty of them doctors, were tried by a US military tribunal for experiments on concentration camp prisoners: freezing, high altitude, malaria, mustard gas, bone grafts and sterilisation. Sixteen were convicted and seven were hanged, including Karl Brandt, Hitler's personal physician. The judgement set out ten principles for permissible experiments. The first says the voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential. The Code had no legal force anywhere, and many American and British researchers assumed it applied to barbarians, not to them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the founding document of research ethics and puts consent first.
spotlights.memory_hook: Rule one of ten: ask, and accept no.

spotlights.name: The Tuskegee syphilis study
spotlights.spot_it: Government doctors drawing blood from Black farmworkers in rural Alabama, who were told they had 'bad blood'.
spotlights.story_md: The US Public Health Service enrolled about 600 Black men in Macon County, Alabama: 399 with latent syphilis and 201 without. They were promised free care, meals and burial insurance. They were never told their diagnosis. When penicillin became the standard cure in the late 1940s, it was deliberately withheld, and the study ran for 40 years. A PHS employee, Peter Buxtun, raised alarms from 1966; the Associated Press reporter Jean Heller broke the story on 25 July 1972. By then dozens of men had died of syphilis, wives had been infected and children born with it. President Clinton apologised in 1997.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the reason modern trials need independent ethics review and why distrust of medicine runs deep in some communities.
spotlights.memory_hook: Forty years of watching, with the cure on the shelf.

spotlights.name: Henry Beecher's 22 examples
spotlights.when: New England Journal of Medicine, June 1966
spotlights.spot_it: A Harvard anaesthetist's short paper listing unethical studies published in leading journals, without names.
spotlights.story_md: Henry Knowles Beecher was no outsider; he was a senior Harvard professor. His 1966 paper 'Ethics and Clinical Research' described 22 studies, chosen from about 50 he had found, in which patients were exposed to risk without consent. Examples included withholding penicillin from soldiers with strep throat and feeding live hepatitis virus to children at the Willowbrook school for the disabled in New York. His point was that the abuses were not done by villains but by respected researchers in mainstream journals. Ironically, Beecher's 1955 paper 'The Powerful Placebo' is also the source of a famous overestimate of the placebo effect.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He showed that unethical research was routine inside respectable medicine, not just in Nazi camps.
spotlights.memory_hook: Twenty-two cases, zero names, and the profession had to look in a mirror.

spotlights.name: Frances Kelsey stops thalidomide
spotlights.spot_it: A Canadian-born FDA reviewer receiving a gold medal from President Kennedy in August 1962.
spotlights.story_md: In September 1960, in her first month at the US Food and Drug Administration, Frances Kelsey was handed an application to sell **thalidomide**, a sleeping pill marketed as Kevadon. It was already sold in about 40 countries. She found the safety data thin and kept asking for more, despite heavy pressure from the company. By late 1961, reports linked the drug to babies born with severe limb defects; worldwide about 10,000 children were affected. The US was largely spared. In October 1962 Congress passed the Kefauver-Harris Amendments, which for the first time required 'adequate and well-controlled investigations' to prove a drug works before sale.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Her refusal and the law that followed made the controlled trial a legal requirement for new drugs.
spotlights.memory_hook: One reviewer said 'not yet' and a nation was spared.

sections.title: How a modern trial works
sections.intro_md:
A new drug today travels a long road. After lab and animal studies come four **phases** of human testing, each with a different question. Before a single patient enrols, the trial must be approved by an independent **ethics committee**, registered in a public database with its main outcome stated in advance, and given a statistical plan.

The second big invention of the late 20th century was the **systematic review**: collecting every trial on a question, not just the famous ones, and combining them in a **meta-analysis**. One trial can be a fluke. Twenty trials pooled together rarely are. The movement that pushed this idea is called **evidence-based medicine**, and its emblem is a small chart that most doctors can now read at a glance.

spotlights.name: Archie Cochrane
spotlights.spot_it: A Scottish doctor and epidemiologist who said medicine should be judged by randomised trials, and who handed out the 'wooden spoon'.
spotlights.story_md: As a prisoner-of-war doctor in Germany in 1941, Cochrane ran a tiny trial of yeast supplements among starving prisoners with swelling legs and saw improvement. He later wrote that he had never been so sure of his own uselessness, since he lacked drugs to treat most patients and many recovered anyway. His 1972 book **Effectiveness and Efficiency** argued that the NHS should pay only for treatments shown to work in RCTs. In 1979 he gave obstetrics the 'wooden spoon' for being the specialty least based on evidence. Obstetricians responded by building the first big database of trials.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He set the agenda of judging all care by the best available trials.
spotlights.memory_hook: A wooden spoon for obstetrics, and obstetrics answered with evidence.

spotlights.name: The Cochrane logo
spotlights.spot_it: Two concentric C shapes enclosing a small chart of horizontal lines and a diamond, beside a vertical line.
spotlights.story_md: The logo is a real **forest plot**. Each horizontal line is one of seven randomised trials of giving corticosteroids to women about to deliver premature babies; the first, by Graham Liggins and Ross Howie in New Zealand in 1972, had been rejected by The Lancet before appearing in Pediatrics. Lines to the left of the vertical line mean fewer babies died. The diamond at the bottom combines them all: a clear benefit. By 1991 the evidence was strong, yet most obstetricians had not adopted the treatment, and tens of thousands of babies probably died or suffered needlessly. A current Cochrane review finds the steroids cut newborn deaths by about 31%.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is a picture of the cost of not pooling evidence.
spotlights.memory_hook: The diamond knew in the 1980s what the wards learned in the 1990s.

spotlights.name: Iain Chalmers
spotlights.spot_it: A British health services researcher who founded the Cochrane Collaboration and the James Lind Library.
spotlights.story_md: Chalmers worked as a doctor in a Palestinian refugee camp in Gaza in the late 1960s and realised that some of what he had been taught was harming his patients. He went on to lead the **Oxford Database of Perinatal Trials** and, in 1993, founded the **Cochrane Collaboration**, an international network that now produces systematic reviews with tens of thousands of volunteer contributors. He later set up the James Lind Library, a free online history of fair tests, and co-wrote the book 'Testing Treatments'. He has argued that unpublished trials are a form of scientific misconduct.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned the idea of systematic reviews into a worldwide institution.
spotlights.memory_hook: He learned in Gaza that his textbooks could kill.

spotlights.name: David Sackett and evidence-based medicine
spotlights.spot_it: A tall Canadian physician in a cardigan, teaching groups of doctors how to appraise a trial.
spotlights.story_md: At McMaster University in Ontario, Sackett built the first department of clinical epidemiology and taught doctors to search, appraise and apply research at the bedside. The term **evidence-based medicine** was coined by his colleague Gordon Guyatt in 1991. In 1994 Sackett moved to Oxford to found the Centre for Evidence-Based Medicine. His definition is still quoted: the conscientious, explicit and judicious use of current best evidence in decisions about individual patients. He also insisted that evidence must be combined with clinical expertise and patients' own values, a part that critics of EBM often forget.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He made reading and judging trials a routine skill for practising doctors.
spotlights.memory_hook: Evidence, expertise and the patient's wishes: three legs, one stool.

sections.title: Treatments that trials killed off
sections.intro_md:
The best argument for trials is the list of treatments that seemed obviously right and were wrong. In each case, doctors had a plausible mechanism, good intentions and observational data that looked convincing. Only randomisation exposed the problem.

The second lesson is darker. A trial only helps if its results are seen. For decades, drug companies and some academics left unfavourable trials unpublished, and regulators sat on data. Estimates over the years have found that about half of completed trials go unreported. That is why the movement for **trial registration** and **open data** matters as much as the method itself.

spotlights.name: CAST: the heart drugs that killed
spotlights.spot_it: A trial of drugs that made irregular heartbeats look better on a monitor while patients died faster.
spotlights.story_md: After a heart attack, extra heartbeats on an ECG predict sudden death. Drugs such as encainide and flecainide suppressed those extra beats beautifully, so doctors prescribed them widely. The **Cardiac Arrhythmia Suppression Trial** randomised about 1,500 patients to drug or placebo. In April 1989 it was stopped early: deaths were about 2.5 times higher on the active drugs. The drugs fixed the number on the screen, a **surrogate endpoint**, while making the outcome that mattered, death, worse. Thomas Moore's book 'Deadly Medicine' estimated tens of thousands of Americans died each year from such drugs before the result.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the textbook warning against trusting a surrogate measure instead of the real outcome.
spotlights.memory_hook: The ECG got better and the patients got buried.

spotlights.name: Hormone therapy and the Women's Health Initiative
spotlights.spot_it: A huge US trial in which older women took a combined hormone pill or a placebo for years.
spotlights.story_md: For decades, observational studies found that women taking hormone replacement therapy after menopause had less heart disease, so millions were prescribed it partly for heart protection. The Women's Health Initiative randomised 16,608 women to oestrogen plus progestin or placebo. In July 2002 the trial was stopped early: the hormone group had more breast cancer, heart attacks, strokes and blood clots. The observational studies had been fooled because women who chose HRT were wealthier and healthier to begin with. Later analyses showed the risks depend on age and timing, and HRT remains a good option for symptoms in younger women.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows how 'healthy user' bias can make a treatment look protective when it is not.
spotlights.memory_hook: The healthy women took the pills; the pills did not make them healthy.

spotlights.name: Fake knee surgery works as well as the real one
spotlights.spot_it: Three small incisions on the knee, the marks of an arthroscopy, real or sham.
spotlights.story_md: Arthroscopic washing and scraping of arthritic knees was among the commonest operations in the US. In 2002 J. Bruce Moseley and colleagues at the Houston Veterans Affairs hospital randomised 180 patients to the real procedure or a **sham**: the same anaesthetic, the same three skin cuts, and the surgeon going through the motions without entering the joint. For two years, patients in both groups reported the same pain and function. A Finnish trial in 2013 found the same for torn meniscus. Earlier, in 1959 and 1960, sham-controlled trials had ended a heart operation, internal mammary artery ligation.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It proved surgery needs placebo controls as much as pills do.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three cuts and nothing inside, and the knees felt just as good.

spotlights.name: Vioxx
spotlights.spot_it: A painkiller, rofecoxib, sold by Merck to millions of arthritis patients as gentler on the stomach.
spotlights.story_md: Vioxx was a blockbuster, with sales of about 2.5 billion dollars a year. Its own large trial, VIGOR, published in 2000, showed about four to five times more heart attacks than with naproxen, which Merck explained as naproxen protecting the heart. Three heart attacks were left out of the published paper. When a later trial against placebo showed doubled cardiovascular risk, Merck withdrew the drug in 2004. FDA scientist David Graham estimated 88,000 to 139,000 extra cases of serious heart disease in the US. Merck later agreed to pay 4.85 billion dollars to settle lawsuits.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows trial data can be spun, and that safety signals must be reported in full.
spotlights.memory_hook: The trial saw the heart attacks; the paper explained them away.

spotlights.name: Tamiflu and the missing data
spotlights.spot_it: A grey and yellow capsule that governments stockpiled by the billion-dollar load against pandemic flu.
spotlights.story_md: Governments, including the UK and US, spent heavily stockpiling oseltamivir, sold by Roche as Tamiflu, for the 2009 swine flu pandemic, on the belief that it reduced complications like pneumonia. Cochrane reviewers asked Roche for the full clinical study reports from 2009. Roche did not provide them, and the BMJ ran a public campaign. In 2013 Roche released 74 full study reports. The 2014 Cochrane review, based on them, found Tamiflu shortened symptoms by about half a day in adults, with no proof that it cut hospital admissions or serious complications. WHO later moved it to its complementary list.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows why full trial reports, not just journal summaries, must be public.
spotlights.memory_hook: Four years to get the data, half a day of benefit.

spotlights.name: Ben Goldacre and AllTrials
spotlights.spot_it: A British doctor and writer with untidy hair who became the public face of the missing-trials problem.
spotlights.story_md: Goldacre wrote the Guardian column 'Bad Science' and the books Bad Science (2008) and **Bad Pharma** (2012). In 2013 he co-founded **AllTrials** with the BMJ, Cochrane, the James Lind Initiative and others, with a simple demand: all trials registered, all results reported. His examples stuck. In the case of the antidepressant reboxetine, published data looked favourable, but most of the patient data had never been published, and the full set showed it was no better than placebo. He later built tools at Oxford to track which trials report on time. Watch his TED talk below.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He turned publication bias from an academic worry into a public scandal.
spotlights.memory_hook: Hidden trials are hidden harms.

sections.title: India and the trial
sections.intro_md:
India's story with clinical trials runs in both directions. Some of the earliest large vaccine tests anywhere were run in British India, and one of the most influential trials of the 20th century was run in Chennai. Indian institutes now run some of the world's biggest vaccine and drug studies, and Indian companies made most of the world's vaccine doses during COVID-19.

There is also a hard chapter. After 2005, rules were loosened to attract global trials, and India became a fast, cheap place to test new drugs. Reports of deaths, poor consent and unpaid compensation led to Supreme Court action in 2013 and a sharp fall in trials. The country rebuilt its system with a public registry, compensation rules and the **New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019**.

spotlights.name: Waldemar Haffkine in Bombay
spotlights.spot_it: A bearded Russian-born scientist in a dark suit, injecting villagers in Calcutta from a syringe.
spotlights.story_md: Haffkine, trained in Odessa and at the Pasteur Institute in Paris, injected himself with his cholera vaccine on 18 July 1892, then came to India in 1893 and vaccinated tens of thousands of people. When plague struck Bombay in 1896 he developed a plague vaccine in a makeshift lab and injected himself on 10 January 1897. At Byculla jail, inmates who volunteered were vaccinated; seven unvaccinated inmates died and none of the vaccinated did. In 1902, 19 villagers in Mulkowal, Punjab, died of tetanus from one contaminated bottle. He was blamed, then cleared. His Bombay lab became the **Haffkine Institute** in 1925.
spotlights.why_it_matters: He ran some of the first large comparative vaccine studies anywhere, in India.
spotlights.memory_hook: He injected himself first, twice.

spotlights.name: The Madras home-versus-sanatorium trial
spotlights.spot_it: Patients with tuberculosis in Chennai's crowded homes, taking pills under supervision instead of going to a sanatorium.
spotlights.story_md: In 1956 the ICMR, WHO and Britain's Medical Research Council set up the **Tuberculosis Chemotherapy Centre** in Madras. Its first trial randomised 193 patients to a year of isoniazid and PAS either at home or in a sanatorium with good food, rest and nursing. Home patients did almost as well; first-year results were around 86% at home against 92% in hospital, relapse later was no worse, and family contacts were not put at greater risk. The study, led by Wallace Fox and others, helped end the sanatorium era worldwide and paved the way for supervised home treatment and later DOTS. The centre is now the ICMR **National Institute for Research in Tuberculosis**.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A Chennai trial changed how the whole world treats tuberculosis.
spotlights.memory_hook: Pills at home did the job of a year in the hills.

spotlights.name: The trial boom, the deaths and the Supreme Court
spotlights.spot_it: Newspaper headlines about poor patients enrolled in foreign drug trials without understanding them.
spotlights.story_md: In 2005 India allowed global trials to run phases in parallel with other countries. Approvals jumped from 65 in 2008 to about 500 in 2010. Investigations, especially in Indore, found patients enrolled without proper consent. Official figures put before Parliament and the Supreme Court reported more than 2,000 deaths of trial participants between 2005 and 2012, of which only a small fraction were judged to be caused by the trials. In 2013 the Supreme Court, hearing **Swasthya Adhikar Manch v. Union of India**, ordered tighter oversight; compensation formulas and audio-visual recording of consent followed, and approvals fell to about 100 in 2013. The **Clinical Trials Registry-India** (CTRI), opened in July 2007, became mandatory in 2009.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that a fair test also needs fair treatment of the people who make it possible.
spotlights.memory_hook: Cheap, fast trials turned out to be expensive in trust.

spotlights.name: The HPV vaccine project and its accidental discovery
spotlights.spot_it: Girls in hostels in Khammam and Vadodara whose vaccinations were halted in 2010, and whose follow-up later changed WHO policy.
spotlights.story_md: In 2009 the NGO PATH, with ICMR and two state governments, gave HPV vaccine to about 23,000 girls aged 10 to 14 in Khammam (then Andhra Pradesh) and Vadodara (Gujarat). Seven girls died; inquiries found the deaths most probably unrelated to the vaccine, but a 2013 parliamentary committee condemned weak consent and oversight. The halt in 2010 also interrupted a separate IARC trial comparing two and three doses, leaving many girls with only one dose. Following them for over a decade showed **one dose protected about as well as two or three**. That finding fed into WHO's single-dose advice, which India used for its national HPV drive launched on 28 February 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: A suspended Indian study accidentally produced one of the most useful vaccine findings of the decade.
spotlights.memory_hook: Stopped by scandal, saved by follow-up: one dose is enough.

spotlights.name: Covaxin's phase 3 trial
spotlights.spot_it: A small glass vial marked BBV152, India's own inactivated COVID-19 vaccine, made by Bharat Biotech in Hyderabad.
spotlights.story_md: Covaxin was developed by Bharat Biotech with the ICMR's National Institute of Virology. On 3 January 2021, India's drug regulator approved it for emergency use 'in clinical trial mode' before phase 3 efficacy results were in, which drew strong criticism from scientists. The phase 3 trial then randomised about 25,800 adults across 25 Indian sites and reported, in The Lancet in November 2021, about 78% efficacy against symptomatic COVID-19. WHO granted emergency use listing in November 2021. The episode is still taught as a case of pressure on the normal order of evidence.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is India's largest home-grown vaccine trial and a lesson in approval before evidence.
spotlights.memory_hook: Approved first, proven later: the order matters.

sections.title: COVID-19: the trial that saved a million lives
sections.intro_md:
When COVID-19 arrived in early 2020, doctors tried everything: antimalarials, HIV drugs, antibiotics, plasma, steroids. Hundreds of small trials started worldwide, most too small to answer anything. Britain did something different. In nine days in March 2020, Oxford researchers designed **RECOVERY**, one simple trial that could run in every NHS hospital, test several drugs at once against usual care, and add or drop drugs as results came in.

It worked spectacularly. Within 100 days it found a cheap drug that saves lives and showed that a much-hyped one does not. Meanwhile, vaccine makers ran the fastest large phase 3 trials in history. The pandemic became a real-world test of whether medicine had learned the lessons of the last 270 years.

visual.title: RECOVERY trial: 28-day deaths, dexamethasone vs usual care (%)

spotlights.name: The RECOVERY trial
spotlights.spot_it: A one-page online form any NHS doctor could fill in at the bedside to randomise a COVID patient.
spotlights.story_md: Led by **Peter Horby** and **Martin Landray**, RECOVERY enrolled its first patient on 19 March 2020 and grew to more than 40,000 patients in 176 UK hospitals, with sites added abroad. On 16 June 2020 it announced that **dexamethasone**, a steroid costing a few pounds a course, cut deaths by about a third in ventilated patients and a fifth in those on oxygen. It was in use worldwide within hours; NHS England later estimated it saved about a million lives globally in nine months. RECOVERY also showed that tocilizumab helps, and that hydroxychloroquine, lopinavir, azithromycin and convalescent plasma do not.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed that a huge, simple trial can find answers in weeks, during a crisis.
spotlights.memory_hook: A cheap old steroid, and a third fewer deaths on ventilators.

spotlights.name: Hydroxychloroquine
spotlights.spot_it: Small white tablets of an old malaria and lupus drug, promoted as a COVID cure by presidents and celebrities.
spotlights.story_md: A small, non-randomised French study in March 2020 and endorsements from US President Donald Trump and Brazil's Jair Bolsonaro turned hydroxychloroquine into a global sensation. India restricted its export and its ICMR recommended it as a preventive for health workers. Lab results looked promising and doctors prescribed it widely. On 5 June 2020, RECOVERY reported its randomised comparison of 1,542 patients on the drug with 3,132 on usual care: 25.7% died on hydroxychloroquine against 23.5% on usual care, no benefit. A major Lancet paper claiming harm had to be retracted, because its data could not be verified.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It shows that hype, small studies and fraud all lose to a large fair test.
spotlights.memory_hook: Presidents prescribed it; randomisation retired it.

spotlights.name: The Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine trial
spotlights.spot_it: A tiny multi-dose glass vial that had to be stored at minus 70 degrees.
spotlights.story_md: The phase 3 trial of BNT162b2, the first mRNA vaccine, enrolled about 43,500 people from July 2020. It was event-driven: the analysis came once enough participants caught COVID. Of 170 confirmed cases, 162 were in the placebo group and 8 in the vaccine group, about 95% efficacy, announced on 9 and 18 November 2020. The trial was fast because it ran phases in parallel and companies manufactured at risk, not because it skipped steps. Rare side effects, such as heart inflammation in young men, surfaced only later in mass use, which is exactly what phase 4 monitoring is for.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It showed a large randomised trial can be done in months when funding and urgency align.
spotlights.memory_hook: 162 against 8.

spotlights.name: Margaret Keenan gets the first jab
spotlights.spot_it: A 90-year-old woman in a blue Christmas penguin T-shirt receiving an injection in Coventry.
spotlights.story_md: At 6.31 in the morning on 8 December 2020, Margaret Keenan, a week short of her 91st birthday, became the first person in the world to receive a clinically authorised, fully tested COVID-19 vaccine outside a trial, at University Hospital Coventry. The second was a man named William Shakespeare. The vial and syringe used on her were given to the Science Museum in London. Her jab marked the end of a sequence that began with trial volunteers, the people who took a dummy injection so that everyone else could know.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the moment trial evidence turned into a public health programme.
spotlights.memory_hook: First Margaret, then Shakespeare.

sections.title: Myths and misreadings
sections.intro_md:
Trials have their own folklore. Some of it is wrong, and some of it is right in a way people do not expect. Here are the claims most worth checking before you repeat them.

**Myth: the placebo effect is huge and works on everything.** Beecher's 1955 claim that placebos help about 35% of patients mixed real placebo effects with natural recovery. A 2001 review by Hróbjartsson and Gøtzsche comparing placebo with no treatment found little evidence of large effects, except modest ones on pain and other self-reported symptoms.

**Myth: 'statistically significant' means important.** A p-value below 0.05 only says the result would be unusual if the treatment did nothing. A tiny, useless effect can be significant in a huge trial. In 2016 the American Statistical Association published a rare formal warning about this.

**Myth: randomised trials are the only real evidence.** Smoking, seatbelts and parachutes were never proven by randomisation. Trials are best for comparing treatments; other designs answer other questions.

spotlights.name: 'First, do no harm' is not in the Oath
spotlights.spot_it: A marble bust of a bearded, balding Greek elder, found in medical schools across the world.
spotlights.story_md: The phrase most associated with medical ethics, 'first, do no harm', is often attributed to the **Hippocratic Oath**. It is not in it. The Latin form 'primum non nocere' seems to date from the 17th to 19th centuries. A related line does appear in another Hippocratic text, Epidemics: practise two things in diseases, to help or not to harm. The Oath itself swears by Apollo and other gods and forbids surgery for stones. The irony for trials: avoiding harm requires knowing which treatments harm, and that requires testing them.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Medicine's most famous ethical rule is misattributed, and it actually demands fair tests.
spotlights.memory_hook: Not in the Oath, but in the logic of every trial.

spotlights.name: Did Lind discover the cure for scurvy?
spotlights.spot_it: Lemons on a tree, the fruit Lind tested and then, in effect, set aside.
spotlights.story_md: Popular accounts say Lind discovered that citrus cures scurvy and the Navy followed. In fact citrus had been recommended long before, by the East India Company surgeon John Woodall in 1617, among others. Lind did not single out citrus as the cure in his conclusions, and he spent years on other explanations. His experiment was rediscovered and celebrated much later, partly because it fits the modern story of the trial. What he deserves credit for is the method: a planned, recorded comparison. Even this is now a myth worth correcting.
spotlights.why_it_matters: History tidies itself up; the real story is better at teaching how evidence spreads.
spotlights.memory_hook: Lind invented the test, not the lemon.

spotlights.name: The p-value
spotlights.spot_it: A number like p = 0.03 printed beside every result in a medical paper.
spotlights.story_md: Fisher suggested 1 in 20, a p-value of 0.05, as a convenient line for when a result is worth a second look. It hardened into a pass mark for publication. Researchers then learned, often unconsciously, to analyse data in many ways until one crossed the line, a practice called **p-hacking**. In 2016 the American Statistical Association warned that a p-value does not measure the size or importance of an effect, nor the probability that the hypothesis is true. Good trials now fix their main outcome and analysis plan in advance and report effect sizes with confidence intervals.
spotlights.why_it_matters: Reading trials well means asking how big an effect is, not only whether it passed a threshold.
spotlights.memory_hook: Significant is not the same as important.

sections.title: What is happening now (2025 to 2026)
sections.intro_md:
The trial is being rebuilt again. The international rulebook for running trials, **ICH E6 Good Clinical Practice**, was rewritten for the first time in decades; the new version, E6(R3), was finalised on 6 January 2025 and took effect in the EU on 23 July 2025. It moves away from box-ticking toward 'quality by design' and allows decentralised trials, with visits at home and data from phones and wearables. The reporting standards for trials, **CONSORT 2025** and **SPIRIT 2025**, were also updated in 2025.

Transparency is back in the news. On 30 March 2026 the US FDA sent reminders to more than 2,200 sponsors linked to over 3,000 trials that appeared to be missing required results on ClinicalTrials.gov; an internal FDA analysis found nearly 30% of trials subject to reporting had no results posted. In India, January 2026 amendments to the NDCT Rules cut some CDSCO approval timelines from 90 days to 45 working days. And on 28 February 2026 India began a national single-dose HPV vaccination drive for 14-year-old girls, built on trial evidence partly gathered in India.

spotlights.name: ICH E6(R3): the new rulebook
spotlights.spot_it: A long guideline document from the International Council for Harmonisation, followed by regulators in the US, EU, Japan, India and elsewhere.
spotlights.story_md: Good Clinical Practice began as a harmonised guideline in 1996. Its third revision keeps the old core, protect participants and produce reliable results, but changes the approach. Sponsors must identify what really matters for a given trial and focus monitoring there, instead of checking every data point. It explicitly accommodates decentralised elements, electronic consent and real-world data, and it treats public registration and reporting of results as part of good practice. The EU applied the principles from 23 July 2025; the US FDA published its version in September 2025. A second annex for pragmatic and decentralised trials was still being finalised in 2026.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It changes how almost every new drug trial in the world is run and checked.
spotlights.memory_hook: Check what matters, not everything.

spotlights.name: The FDA's results-reporting reminders
spotlights.spot_it: Emails from the US drug regulator telling sponsors their trial results are overdue on ClinicalTrials.gov.
spotlights.story_md: US law has required many trials to post results on ClinicalTrials.gov within a year of completion since 2007, with fines possible since 2017. Enforcement was rare. On 30 March 2026 the FDA contacted more than 2,200 sponsors and investigators about more than 3,000 trials that appeared to lack required results or had failed quality checks, and it disclosed this on 13 April 2026. These were reminders, not formal notices of non-compliance, but they signalled that the agency may escalate. The registry itself lists more than half a million studies from over 200 countries.
spotlights.why_it_matters: It is the clearest sign in years that regulators intend to enforce trial transparency.
spotlights.memory_hook: Three thousand trials, one reminder: publish.

spotlights.name: India's 2026 trial rule changes
spotlights.spot_it: A government gazette amendment to India's New Drugs and Clinical Trials Rules, 2019.
spotlights.story_md: The 2019 rules already set timelines: 30 working days for trials of drugs developed in India, 90 for others, plus compensation for trial injury and registration of ethics committees. The January 2026 amendments cut CDSCO's turnaround for certain applications, such as licences to manufacture new or investigational drugs for trials, from 90 days to 45 working days. They also created a 'prior intimation' route under which some applicants can start once acknowledged, and waived prior permission for some low-risk bioequivalence studies. Further drafts in early 2026 proposed changes to animal toxicity testing and ethics committee registration.
spotlights.why_it_matters: India is trying to speed up research without repeating the failures of the 2005 to 2012 boom.
spotlights.memory_hook: Faster approvals, same promise of safety: the test is in the doing.

sections.title: Recap: how medicine learned to test itself
sections.intro_md:
Medicine learned to test itself in steps, and each step was a reaction to being fooled.

1. **Compare.** Lind's six pairs (1747) showed the power of a planned comparison.
2. **Count.** Louis, Semmelweis, Snow and Nightingale replaced memorable cases with rates.
3. **Blind.** Franklin's commission (1784) and Haygarth's wooden tractors (1799) showed that expectation alone can cure symptoms.
4. **Randomise.** Fibiger alternated, Fisher proved why chance matters, and Bradford Hill's sealed envelopes (1948) made it routine.
5. **Scale.** The 1954 polio trial and RECOVERY in 2020 showed big, simple trials can settle questions fast.
6. **Protect.** Nuremberg, Tuskegee and thalidomide forced consent, ethics review and proof of efficacy into law.
7. **Pool and publish.** Cochrane's forest plot and AllTrials showed that evidence is only as good as the share of it you can see.

The India thread runs through it: Haffkine's vaccines, the Madras TB trial, the 2013 reckoning, Covaxin and a single-dose HPV finding that now protects girls across the country.

cards.front: When and where did Lind run his scurvy test?
cards.back: 20 May 1747, aboard HMS Salisbury in the Bay of Biscay: 12 sailors, 6 pairs.

cards.front: Which of Lind's six treatments worked best?
cards.back: Two oranges and a lemon a day.

cards.front: Who is this naval surgeon?
cards.back: James Lind (1716 to 1794).

cards.front: When did the Royal Navy issue lemon juice fleet-wide?
cards.back: 1795, 48 years after Lind's test.

cards.front: Why does randomisation matter more than matching groups by age and sex?
cards.back: Chance also balances the factors you cannot see or did not think to measure.

cards.front: What is double blinding?
cards.back: Neither patients nor the people assessing outcomes know who got the real treatment.

cards.front: Placebo is Latin for '___'.
cards.back: I shall please.

cards.front: What did Daniel propose to the king's steward?
cards.back: A ten-day test: vegetables and water against the royal food, then compare.

cards.front: What did Paré use when the boiling oil ran out at Turin in 1537?
cards.back: A dressing of egg yolk, oil of roses and turpentine. Those soldiers did better.

cards.front: What kind of manuscript is this, written by Ibn Sina around 1025?
cards.back: The Canon of Medicine, which set out rules for testing drugs.

cards.front: How was George Washington treated for his fatal sore throat in 1799?
cards.back: He was bled four times, about 2.4 litres, and died that night.

cards.front: What did Pierre Louis show in 1835?
cards.back: Counting outcomes in pneumonia patients, he found bloodletting did far less good than believed.

cards.front: Who is this Hungarian doctor who brought in chlorine handwashing?
cards.back: Ignaz Semmelweis.

cards.front: What does this 1854 map show?
cards.back: John Snow's map of cholera deaths clustered round the Broad Street pump.

cards.front: Whose chart is this, and what did its big wedges show?
cards.back: Florence Nightingale's 1858 rose diagram: disease killed far more soldiers than wounds.

cards.front: What is this tub with iron rods?
cards.back: Mesmer's baquet, used for 'animal magnetism' cures.

cards.front: Who sat on the 1784 commission that invented blind testing?
cards.back: Benjamin Franklin, Antoine Lavoisier and Joseph-Ignace Guillotin, among others.

cards.front: What did Haygarth make in 1799, and what happened?
cards.back: Wooden fake Perkins tractors. Four of five patients felt relief, as with the real ones.

cards.front: What are these metal rods?
cards.back: Perkins's 'metallic tractors', patented in 1796.

cards.front: How did Fibiger allocate diphtheria serum in 1896 to 1897?
cards.back: By alternate days of admission. 8 serum patients died against 30 controls.

cards.front: Who is this statistician, author of The Design of Experiments (1935)?
cards.back: Ronald Fisher.

cards.front: What is this field, and why does it matter to medicine?
cards.back: Broadbalk at Rothamsted, where Fisher learned why experiments need randomisation.

cards.front: What is usually called the first properly randomised medical trial?
cards.back: The MRC streptomycin trial for tuberculosis, published 30 October 1948.

cards.front: How was allocation hidden in the 1948 trial?
cards.back: Random numbers in sealed, opaque envelopes, opened only after enrolment.

cards.front: Who is this statistician who designed the 1948 trial?
cards.back: Sir Austin Bradford Hill.

cards.front: What did the British Doctors Study find?
cards.back: Smokers died about ten years earlier than non-smokers.

cards.front: How many children were in the 1954 polio vaccine trial?
cards.back: About 1.8 million.

cards.front: Who is this virologist, asked 'who owns the patent'?
cards.back: Jonas Salk: 'Could you patent the sun?'

cards.front: What was the Cutter incident?
cards.back: In 1955 some vaccine batches still held live virus, paralysing and killing children; batch testing followed.

cards.front: What is the first principle of the Nuremberg Code (1947)?
cards.back: The voluntary consent of the human subject is absolutely essential.

cards.front: How long did the Tuskegee syphilis study run, and what was withheld?
cards.back: 1932 to 1972; penicillin was withheld after it became the standard cure.

cards.front: Who is receiving this award from President Kennedy in 1962?
cards.back: Frances Kelsey, the FDA reviewer who kept thalidomide off the US market.

cards.front: What did the 1962 Kefauver-Harris Amendments require?
cards.back: Proof of effectiveness through adequate and well-controlled investigations before a drug is sold.

cards.front: Name the four phases of clinical trials and their main question.
cards.back: 1: safety and dose. 2: early efficacy and side effects. 3: better than current care? 4: long-term and rare harms after approval.

cards.front: What is the chart inside this logo?
cards.back: A forest plot of trials of steroids before premature birth.

cards.front: Who is this, founder of the Cochrane Collaboration in 1993?
cards.back: Sir Iain Chalmers.

cards.front: Who coined 'evidence-based medicine', and when?
cards.back: Gordon Guyatt at McMaster, 1991; David Sackett championed it.

cards.front: Why did CAST matter beyond heart drugs?
cards.back: It showed that improving a surrogate measure (extra beats) can worsen the real outcome (death).

cards.front: Why did observational studies wrongly suggest HRT protected the heart?
cards.back: Women who chose HRT were healthier and wealthier to begin with: healthy-user bias.

cards.front: What drug was sold in this pack, withdrawn in 2004?
cards.back: Vioxx (rofecoxib), withdrawn over heart attack risk.

cards.front: Who is this doctor who co-founded AllTrials in 2013?
cards.back: Ben Goldacre.

cards.front: Who is this scientist who tested plague vaccine in Bombay in 1897?
cards.back: Waldemar Haffkine.

cards.front: What did the 1956 Madras TB trial compare, and find?
cards.back: Home treatment against sanatorium care: home patients did almost as well.

cards.front: What is CTRI?
cards.back: The Clinical Trials Registry-India, opened July 2007, mandatory from 2009.

cards.front: What did RECOVERY find about dexamethasone in June 2020?
cards.back: It cut deaths by about a third on ventilators and a fifth on oxygen.

cards.front: Whose first-ever authorised COVID jab used this vial and syringe?
cards.back: Margaret Keenan, 8 December 2020, Coventry.

cards.front: Why did William Gosset publish as 'Student'?
cards.back: His employer, the Guinness brewery, did not let staff publish under their own names.

cards.front: What statistical test did Gosset invent for small samples?
cards.back: Student's t-test (1908), first used for barley and beer quality.

cards.front: A p-value below 0.05 does not mean the effect is ___.
cards.back: Large or important.

cards.front: Whose bust is this, and which famous phrase is wrongly attributed to his Oath?
cards.back: Hippocrates; 'first, do no harm' is not in the Oath.

quiz_bank.explanation: He believed scurvy had several causes and kept exploring other ideas.

quiz_bank.explanation: Balance known and unknown factors between groups.

quiz_bank.explanation: Both patients and those assessing outcomes.

quiz_bank.prompt: What standard treatment did Paré abandon after Turin in 1537?
quiz_bank.explanation: Pouring boiling oil into gunshot wounds.

quiz_bank.prompt: Pierre Louis's 1835 study counted outcomes of:

quiz_bank.prompt: Snow's strongest evidence came from comparing households served by two different water companies.
quiz_bank.explanation: His 'grand experiment' in south London.

quiz_bank.prompt: What happened to the boy in Franklin's garden at Passy?
quiz_bank.explanation: He fainted at an apricot tree that had not been magnetised.

quiz_bank.prompt: Haygarth's fake tractors were made of:

quiz_bank.prompt: Fisher's 'lady tasting tea' test used how many cups?

quiz_bank.prompt: Fibiger's diphtheria trial allocated serum by flipping a coin for each patient.

quiz_bank.prompt: In the 1948 trial, allocations were kept in:
quiz_bank.explanation: Sealed opaque envelopes.

quiz_bank.prompt: The British Doctors Study randomised doctors to smoke or not.
quiz_bank.explanation: It was an observational cohort; you cannot ethically randomise smoking.

quiz_bank.prompt: On which date was the polio vaccine announced as safe and effective?
quiz_bank.explanation: 12 April 1955, ten years after Roosevelt's death.

quiz_bank.prompt: The Cutter incident was caused by:
quiz_bank.explanation: Vaccine batches in which the virus had not been fully inactivated.

quiz_bank.prompt: The Nuremberg Code was immediately binding law in the US and UK.
quiz_bank.explanation: It had no direct legal force; many researchers thought it did not apply to them.

quiz_bank.prompt: Who broke the Tuskegee story in 1972?

quiz_bank.prompt: Before 1962, US drug law mainly required companies to show a drug was:

quiz_bank.prompt: Which phase usually involves thousands of patients randomised against current care?
quiz_bank.explanation: Phase 3.

quiz_bank.prompt: In a forest plot, the diamond at the bottom shows:

quiz_bank.prompt: CAST showed that anti-arrhythmic drugs after heart attacks:
quiz_bank.explanation: Increased deaths despite suppressing extra beats.

quiz_bank.prompt: Haffkine tested his plague vaccine on himself before using it in Bombay.
