best_facts.fact: A Danish trial in 1898 that alternated diphtheria serum by day of admission is now praised as a model of fair testing, while its author's 1926 Nobel Prize was for a cancer 'discovery' that turned out to be wrong.
best_facts.why_surprising: The Nobel work failed; the overlooked trial endured.

best_facts.fact: When India's HPV vaccine studies were halted in 2010, many girls ended up with only one dose. Following them for over a decade showed one dose protected about as well as three, evidence that fed WHO's single-dose advice and India's 2026 national drive.
best_facts.why_surprising: A scandal-stopped study produced one of the decade's most useful vaccine findings.

best_facts.fact: The first blind test in medicine was run in 1784 by a commission including Benjamin Franklin and Antoine Lavoisier, to debunk Mesmer's 'animal magnetism'. A boy fainted under the wrong, unmagnetised tree.
best_facts.why_surprising: Blinding was invented to catch a fraud, not to test a drug.

best_facts.fact: In 1799 John Haygarth made fake Perkins tractors out of painted wood. Four of his five rheumatism patients reported relief, just as with the patented metal ones.
best_facts.why_surprising: The placebo control predates the stethoscope.

best_facts.fact: Lind proved citrus cured scurvy in 1747, but the Royal Navy issued lemon juice to the whole fleet only in 1795, 48 years later.
best_facts.why_surprising: Proof and policy were half a century apart.

best_facts.fact: Arthroscopic knee surgery for arthritis did no better than a sham operation, three skin cuts with nothing done inside, in a 2002 trial of 180 patients.
best_facts.why_surprising: Surgery can be a placebo too.

best_facts.fact: The Cochrane logo is a real forest plot of trials of steroids for women in premature labour. The benefit was clear for years before most obstetricians used them.
best_facts.why_surprising: A logo is a monument to babies who need not have died.

best_facts.fact: The heart drugs tested in CAST made irregular beats look better on the monitor while raising deaths about 2.5-fold, so the trial was stopped early in 1989.
best_facts.why_surprising: Fixing the number on the screen killed the patient.

best_facts.fact: In 1948 Britain could afford so little streptomycin that rationing was unavoidable; Bradford Hill argued that drawing lots was the fairest way to ration it, and that created the first modern RCT.
best_facts.why_surprising: A shortage made the control group ethical.

best_facts.fact: Austin Bradford Hill, who designed modern clinical trials, had no medical degree. Tuberculosis caught as a First World War pilot ended his plan to become a doctor.
best_facts.why_surprising: The father of the medical trial was not a doctor.

best_facts.fact: Dexamethasone, a steroid costing a few pounds a course, cut COVID deaths among ventilated patients by about a third; NHS England estimated it saved about a million lives in nine months.
best_facts.why_surprising: The pandemic's best early drug was cheap and old.

best_facts.fact: 'First, do no harm' is not in the Hippocratic Oath.
best_facts.why_surprising: Medicine's most quoted rule is misattributed.

best_facts.fact: Fisher designed the logic of modern experiments around a woman who claimed she could taste whether milk or tea was poured first: eight cups, four of each, in random order.
best_facts.why_surprising: A tea party built the p-value.

best_facts.fact: In Snow's 1854 'grand experiment', houses supplied by a company drawing sewage-tainted Thames water had about 315 cholera deaths per 10,000 against 37 for its upstream rival, often on the same street.
best_facts.why_surprising: History ran a randomised trial before the germ was seen.

best_facts.fact: In Vienna, mothers begged to give birth in the street rather than in the doctors' maternity ward, which killed about five times as many as the midwives' ward until handwashing came in.
Haffkine injected himself with his own cholera vaccine in 1892 and his plague vaccine in 1897 before testing them in India.
best_facts.why_surprising: The first volunteer was the inventor.

best_facts.fact: A 1956 Chennai trial showed tuberculosis patients treated at home did almost as well as those in sanatoria, helping end the sanatorium era worldwide.
best_facts.why_surprising: A Madras study changed global TB care.

best_facts.fact: Of 170 COVID cases in the Pfizer-BioNTech phase 3 trial, 162 were in the placebo group and 8 in the vaccine group.
best_facts.why_surprising: A whole pandemic decision rested on 170 people.

side_dish.title: The brewer who taught science to trust small samples
side_dish.body_md:
In 1899 the Guinness brewery in Dublin hired a young Oxford chemistry graduate, **William Sealy Gosset**, to improve its beer. Guinness wanted to know which barley varieties and which hops gave the most reliable stout. The trouble was that brewing experiments are small. You cannot plant a thousand fields or brew a thousand batches, and the statistics of the day assumed huge samples.

Gosset worked out how much chance variation to expect when you only have a handful of measurements. The result, published in 1908, is the **t-distribution**, and the test built on it is still the most used in medical research. Every time a small trial compares the average of two groups, it is likely using his maths.

There was a catch. Guinness had been burned when another employee published trade secrets, so staff were not allowed to publish under their own names. Gosset signed his paper **'Student'**, and it has been 'Student's t-test' ever since.

Gosset became a friend and sparring partner of Ronald Fisher, who extended his work and built it into the design of experiments. In the photograph with this note, the two men stand beside a bicycle. One made beer, the other studied wheat, and between them they gave medicine the tools to decide, from a few dozen patients, whether a treatment really works.

offline_task.title: Run a blind taste test at home
offline_task.body_md:
Recreate Fisher's 'lady tasting tea' with something you think you can tell apart: two brands of cola, filter versus instant coffee, tea with milk poured first or second, or bottled versus tap water.

1. Prepare **eight** identical cups, four of each kind. Mark the bottoms, not the sides.
2. Ask someone else to shuffle them, so you do not know the order. That is randomisation and blinding.
3. Taste each and write your guess before turning the cup over.
4. Score yourself. Getting all eight right by pure guessing happens only about once in 70 tries, so it is real evidence. Six out of eight is far less impressive than it feels.
5. Now swap roles. Watch how hard it is not to give hints when you know the answer. That is why trials blind the assessors too.

Note what surprised you: most people are more confident than their score justifies, which is exactly why medicine had to learn to test itself.
